19       Pending before the Court is Third-Party Defendant Angela Hong’s (“Ms. Hong”) 
20  Motion to Dismiss the Hortman Parties’ Third-Party Complaint (“Motion to Dismiss”), 
21  which was filed on August 12, 2024.  (Doc. 223.)  On August 30, 2024, Third-Party 
22  Plaintiffs Kim Buhler, administrator and executor of the Estate of Barbara Hortman, and 
23  Kim Buhler and Norman Alton Hortman, III, Trustees of the Norman Alton Hortman and 
24  Barbara Hortman Revocable Trust No. 1 Dated July 2, 1985 (the “Hortman Parties”) filed 
25  an  Opposition  to  Ms.  Hong’s  Motion  to  Dismiss  (“Opposition”).    (Doc.  229.)    On 
26  September 9, 2024, Ms. Hong filed a Reply in Support of her Motion to Dismiss (“Reply”).  
27  (Doc. 235.)                                                               
28                                                                            
1       The  Court  finds  this  matter  suitable  for  determination  without  oral  argument 
2  pursuant to Civil Local Rule 7.1(d)(1).  For the reasons discussed below, Ms. Hong’s 
3  Motion to Dismiss is DENIED.                                              
4                           I.   BACKGROUND                                  
5  A.   Factual Background                                                   
6       1.   Plaintiff and the 1680 Property                                 
7       Plaintiff  Pacific  Resources  Associates  LLC  (“Pacific  Resources”)  owned  the 
8  property located at 1680 East Valley Parkway, Escondido, California 92027, a storefront 
9  in the Valley Plaza shopping center, from February 12, 2001 until November 2022 (the 
10  “1680 Property”).  (Doc. 114 at 9.)                                       
11       2.   M&E, the Barawids, the Hortman Parties, and the 1718 Property   
12       M&E Brothers, LLC (“M&E”) owns the property located at 1718 East Valley 
13  Parkway, Escondido, California 92027, another storefront in the Valley Plaza shopping 
14  center (the “1718 Property”).  (Case No. 3:22-cv-01892-RBM-DEB, Doc. 13 at 2.)  The 
15  1718 Property is located east of Plaintiff’s 1680 Property.  (Doc. 223 at 9.)  M&E acquired 
16  the 1718 Property from Michael L. Barawid, Edward L. Barawid, and Flor De Lys L. 
17  Barawid (the “Barawids”) on December 29, 2004.  (Case No. 3:22-cv-01892-RBM-DEB, 
18  Doc. 13 at 2.)  The Hortman Parties held title to the 1718 Property between September 3, 
19  1987 and August 17, 1999.  (Id.)                                          
20       3.   The Kims and the 1654 Property                                  
21       Guhn Y. Kim and Yun Soon Kim, individually and as husband and wife, and Guhn 
22  Y. Kim and Yun Soon Kim, as trustees of The Kim Family Trust of 2017 (collectively, 
23  “the Kims”) own the property located at 1654 East Valley Parkway, Escondido, California 
24  92027, a third storefront in the Valley Plaza shopping center (the “1654 Property”).  (Case 
25  No. 3:22-cv-01892-RBM-DEB, Doc. 34 at 46–47.)  The 1654 Property is located west of 
26  Plaintiff’s 1680 Property.  (Doc. 223 at 9.)  The 1654 Property is currently home to Suzy 
27  Cleaners.  (Case No. 3:22-cv-01892-RBM-DEB, Doc. 34 at 46–47.)            
28                                                                            
1  B.   Procedural History                                                   
2       1.   The 2020 Pacific Resources Action                               
3       Pacific Resources initially filed this case on February 6, 2020—over four years ago.  
4  (Doc. 1.)  Pacific Resources then amended its Complaint on February 3, 2023 (Doc. 83) 
5  and on May 1, 2023 (Doc. 114).  Pacific Resources alleged that the former and current 
6  owners and operators of the drycleaning businesses located at the 1654 Property and the 
7  1718 Property released perchloroethylene (“PCE”) into the soil beneath the properties, 
8  which then migrated and contaminated the soil beneath Pacific Resource’s 1680 Property.  
9  (Id. at 9–11.)  Pacific Resources alleged that it incurred substantial response, removal, and 
10  remediation costs.  (Id. at 10–13.)  Pacific Resources asserted three causes of action under 
11  the federal Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act 
12  (“CERCLA”), one cause of action under California’s Hazardous Substances Account Act 
13  (“HSAA”), and nine additional tort and equitable causes of action under California state 
14  common law.  (Id. at 13–26.)  Pacific Resources has since settled all of its claims.  (See 
15  Doc. 168, 169, 195.)                                                      
16       On April 27, 2023, the Kims, the owners of the 1654 Property, answered Pacific 
17  Resource’s Second Amended Complaint, denying all liability.  (Doc. 115.)  The Kims also 
18  filed third-party claims against M&E, the Barawids, the Hortman Parties, and other former 
19  owners and operators of the drycleaning businesses previously located at the 1718 Property 
20  for (1) contribution under CERCLA, (2) equitable indemnity, (3) indemnity/contribution 
21  under the HSAA, (4) federal declaratory relief, (5) state law contribution, (6) trespass, and 
22  (7) private nuisance.  (Doc. 115 at 17–27.)                               
23       Likewise, on  May  19,  2023,  the Hortman  Parties  answered  Pacific Resources’ 
24  Second Amended Complaint, denying all liability.  (Doc. 129.)  Additionally, the Hortman 
25  Parties filed crossclaims for contribution and/or indemnity under CERCLA, HSAA, and 
26  California Civil Code section 1432 against the Kims and M&E, among others.  (Doc. 129 
27  at 32.)  The Hortman Parties also filed a Third-Party Complaint against prior owners and 
28  operators of the 1718 Property dating back to the 1960s for contribution and/or indemnity 
1  under CERCLA, HSAA, and California Civil Code section 1432.  (Doc. 129 at 48–63.)   
2       2.   The 2022 M&E Action                                             
3       On November 30, 2022, Defendant M&E filed a separate action against the Hortman 
4  Parties (Case No. 22-cv-01892-RBM-DEB, Doc. 1), which it then amended on March 22, 
5  2023 (Case No. 22-cv-01892-RBM-DEB, Doc. 13).  M&E contends that it is entitled to 
6  the recovery of response costs and contribution for the investigation and cleanup of its 1718 
7  Property (id. at 12–15, 23), as well as damages for negligence, nuisance, trespass, and 
8  waste (id. at 16–24).                                                     
9  C.   The Hortman Parties’ Third-Party Complaint                           
10       On June 13, 2024, in response to M&E’s separate action against them, the Hortman 
11  Parties’ filed a Third-Party Complaint against Ms. Hong, among many others.  (See Case 
12  No. 3:22-cv-01892-RBM-DEB [“Hortman Parties’ Third-Party Complaint”], Doc. 34 at 
13  44–73.)  The Hortman Parties’ Third-Party Complaint is the subject of Ms. Hong’s Motion 
14  to Dismiss and this Order.                                                
15       In their Third-Party Complaint, the Hortman Parties allege that Ms. Hong has owned 
16  and operated the drycleaning business located on the 1654 Property since approximately 
17  December 25, 2001.  (Hortman Parties’ Third-Party Complaint ¶ 14.)  Ms. Hong is referred 
18  to as an “Operator” Third-Party Defendant throughout the Hortman Parties’ Third-Party 
19  Complaint.  (Id.)                                                         
20       1.   Group Allegations                                               
21       The  Hortman  Parties  allege  that  “the  Operator  Third-Party  Defendants  leased, 
22  owned and/or operated dry cleaning facilities on the 1654 Property or 1718 Property[.]”  
23  (Id. ¶ 55.)  The Hortman Parties allege that the Site, which includes the 1654 Property, the 
24  1680 Property, the 1718 Property, and adjacent properties, “has been impacted by the 
25  presence  of  Hazardous  Substances  including,  but  not  limited  to,  volatile  organic 
26  compounds (‘VOCs’) such as tetrachloroethylene, or PCE.”  (Id. ¶ 56.)  The Hortman 
27  Parties allege “that VOCs, including PCE, were detected above laboratory reporting limits 
28  in the soil vapor approximately 5-feet below ground surface (bgs) beneath the 1654 
1  Property, the 1680 Property, and the 1718 Property in 2022.”  (Id.)  The Hortman Parties 
2  allege “that PCE was detected above the laboratory reporting limit in the groundwater 
3  approximately 15-feet bgs beneath the 1718 Property in 2022.”  (Id.)      
4       The Hortman Parties allege that “Third-Party Defendants’ handling, generation, 
5  usage, storage, disposal or Release of Hazardous Substances and Hazardous Waste at the 
6  1654 and 1718 Properties or adjacent sites has caused contamination and pollution of 
7  structures, soil, subsoils, surface water and groundwater at and in the vicinity of the Site 
8  and has resulted in further release, spread and co-mingling of contamination.”  (Id. ¶ 57.)  
9       The Hortman Parties allege that “Third-Party Defendants exercised oversight of the 
10  management  and  control  of  Hazardous  Substance  and  Hazardous  Waste  activities 
11  conducted thereon, or arranged for the Disposal of Hazardous Substances at the 1654 and 
12  1718 Properties, are parties who are liable or potentially liable for any necessary costs of 
13  response incurred for the investigation and remediation of any and all Disposals and/or 
14  Releases of Hazardous Substances at the Site.”  (Id. ¶ 59.)               
15       The Hortman Parties allege that “each Third-Party Defendant caused or contributed 
16  to the past or present handling, storage, treatment, transportation, generation, Release, or 
17  Disposal  of  Hazardous  Substances,  Hazardous  Waste,  and/or  solid  waste  in  the 
18  Environment in, at, and around the Site, including soil, land, subsurface strata, air, vapor, 
19  groundwater, surface water, and the waters of the state of California, because each Third-
20  Party  Defendant  Released  or  otherwise  discarded  Hazardous  Substances,  Hazardous 
21  Waste, and/or solid waste, or controlled and/or operated the Site and business from which 
22  Hazardous Substances, Hazardous Waste, and/or solid waste were Released or otherwise 
23  discarded, and failed to prevent or abate the Hazardous Substances, Hazardous Waste, 
24  and/or solid waste contamination.”  (Id. ¶ 60.)                           
25       The Hortman Parties allege that “Third-Party Defendants intentionally, negligently, 
26  suddenly, and accidentally caused or contributed to the presence of Hazardous Substances, 
27  Hazardous Waste, and/or solid waste in the Environment, including soil, land, subsurface 
28  strata, air, vapor, groundwater, surface water, and the waters of the state of California, at 
1  the Site by their respective operations of the dry cleaning machine(s), lack of maintenance 
2  and/or  improper  Disposal  of  PCE  waste,  amongst  other  operational  practices.  Once 
3  released into the Environment, these Hazardous Substances, Hazardous Waste, and/or solid 
4  wastes have continued to spread and migrate within the Environment at the Site, but Third-
5  Party Defendants failed to abate this contamination.”  (Id. ¶ 62.)        
6       2.   Specific Allegations                                            
7       The Hortman Parties allege that Ms. Hong used PCE for drycleaning at the 1654 
8  Property until 2013.  (Id. ¶ 62.)  Plaintiffs allege that Ms. Hong was “required to conduct 
9  weekly vapor and leak checks and record the date performed and related components 
10  repaired  on  a  San  Diego  County  Air  Pollution  Control  District  [‘APCD’]  approved 
11  checklist as a condition of their respective permits during their PCE drycleaning operations 
12  on the 1654 Property.”  (Id.)                                             
13       The Hortman Parties allege that Ms. Hong “received notices of violation for PCE 
14  vapor leaks on the 1654 Property from the San Diego County Air Pollution Control District 
15  during her operation of Suzy Cleaners in 2003 and 2004” and that her “drycleaning 
16  machine was leaking on the 1654 Property in September 2005.”  (Id. ¶ 68 (emphasis 
17  added).)  The Hortman Parties allege that Ms. Hong “was responsible for the disposal of 
18  spent dry cleaning fluids containing PCE during her operation of Suzy Cleaners.”  (Id. 
19  ¶ 69.)                                                                    
20       3.   Causes of Action                                                
21       The Hortman Parties assert four causes of action against Ms. Hong: (1) Contribution 
22  Pursuant to CERCLA § 113(f), 42 U.S.C. § 9613(f); (2) Declaratory Relief Under Federal 
23  Law; (3) Indemnity/Contribution Under the HSAA, Health & Safety Code § 25363(a); and 
24  (4) Cost Recovery Pursuant to CERCLA § 107, 42 U.S.C. § 9607.             
25  D.   Ms. Hong’s Motion to Dismiss                                         
26       In her Motion to Dismiss, Ms. Hong argues that “the only relevant question on this 
27  Motion [to Dismiss] is whether the [Third-Party] Complaint adequately alleges that Ms. 
28  Hong is liable as a ‘covered person’ under [CERCLA]” because the Hortman Parties’ 
1  claims under HSAA and for federal declaratory relief are both contingent upon  their 
2  CERCLA claims.  (Doc. 223 at 13–14.)                                      
3       Ms. Hong asserts that “covered persons” include: “1) an owner or operator of a 
4  facility; 2) any person who at the time of disposal of hazardous substance owned or 
5  operated a facility at which such hazardous substances were disposed of [i.e., a past owner 
6  or operator]; 3) any person who by contract, agreement, or otherwise arranged for disposal 
7  or  treatment  of  hazardous  substances  at  a  facility;  and  4)  any  person  who  accepted 
8  hazardous substances for transport to disposal at a facility or site from which there is a 
9  release.”  (Id. at 14 (citing 42 U.S.C. § 9607(a)(1)–(4)).                
10       Ms. Hong then argues that the Hortman Parties’ Third-Party Complaint does not 
11  adequately allege (1) that Ms. Hong is a current owner or operator (id. at 15–16), (2) that 
12  the disposal of hazardous substances occurred at the facility during her operation (id. at 
13  16–20), or (3) that she arranged for disposal of hazardous substances at a facility (id. at 20–
14  21).  In making her second argument regarding the disposal of hazardous substances that 
15  occurred at the facility during her operation, Ms. Hong asserts that the Court may consider 
16  the APCD checklists in ruling on her Motion to Dismiss because they are referenced in the 
17  Hortman Parties’ Third-Party Complaint, they are central to the Hortman Parties’ claims, 
18  and their authenticity is not questioned.  (Doc. 223 at 19–20.)  Interpreting the information 
19  from the 2005 checklist, Ms. Hong argues that each of the reported “leaks,” even the leak 
20  in  2005,  was  merely  a  “vapor  leak,”  which  does  not  constitute  a  “disposal”  under 
21  CERCLA.  (Id. at 16–19.)                                                  
22       The Hortman Parties respond that they have sufficiently alleged that Ms. Hong was 
23  both a current and past operator of the drycleaning business at the 1654 Property.  (Doc. 
24  229 at 7, 9–12.)                                                          
25                         II.  LEGAL STANDARD                                
26       Pursuant to Rule 12(b)(6), an action may be dismissed for failure to allege “enough 
27  facts to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.”  Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 
28  U.S. 544, 570 (2007).  “A claim has facial plausibility when the plaintiff pleads factual 
1  content that allows the court to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is liable 
2  for  the  misconduct  alleged.   The  plausibility  standard  is  not  akin to a 
3  probability requirement, but it asks for more than a sheer possibility that a defendant acted 
4  unlawfully.”  Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009) (internal quotation marks and 
5  citations omitted).  For purposes of ruling on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, the Court “accept[s] 
6  factual allegations in the complaint as true and construe[s] the pleadings in the light most 
7  favorable to the nonmoving party.”  Manzarek v. St. Paul Fire & Marine Ins. Co., 519 F.3d 
8  1025, 1031 (9th Cir. 2008).                                               
9       However, the Court is “not bound to accept as true a legal conclusion couched as a 
10  factual allegation.”  Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 678 (quoting Twombly, 550 U.S. at 555).  Nor is the 
11  Court  “required  to  accept  as  true  allegations  that  contradict  exhibits  attached  to  the 
12  [c]omplaint or matters properly subject to judicial notice, or allegations that are merely 
13  conclusory, unwarranted deductions of fact, or unreasonable inferences.”  Daniels-Hall v. 
14  Nat’l Educ. Ass’n, 629 F.3d 992, 998 (9th Cir. 2010).  “In sum, for a complaint to survive 
15  a motion to dismiss, the non-conclusory factual content, and reasonable inferences from 
16  that content, must be plausibly suggestive of a claim entitling the plaintiff to relief.”  Moss 
17  v. U.S. Secret Serv., 572 F.3d 962, 969 (9th Cir. 2009) (quotation marks omitted). 
18       When a Rule 12(b)(6) motion is granted, “a district court should grant leave to amend 
19  even if no request to amend the pleading was made, unless it determines that the pleading 
20  could not possibly be cured by the allegation of other facts.”  Cook, Perkiss & Liehe v. N. 
21  Cal. Collection Serv., 911 F.2d 242, 247 (9th Cir. 1990) (citations omitted).   
22                            III.  DISCUSSION                                
23       “In order to prevail in a private action under CERCLA for response costs or natural 
24  resource damages, a plaintiff must prove the following elements, among others: (1) the site 
25  on  which  the  hazardous  substances  are  found  is  a  ‘facility’  within  the  meaning  of 
26  CERCLA, 42 U.S.C. § 9601(9); (2) a ‘release’ or ‘threatened release’ of any ‘hazardous 
27  substance’ from the facility has occurred, 42 U.S.C. § 9607(a)(4); and (3) the defendant is 
28  within one of the four broad classes of ‘potentially responsible parties’ (‘PRPs’) listed in 
1  42 U.S.C. § 9607(a)(1)–(4).”  Pakootas v. Teck Cominco Metals, LTD., 830 F.3d 975, 981 
2  (9th Cir. 2016) (citing 3550 Stevens Creek Assocs. v. Barclays Bank of Cal., 915 F.2d 1355, 
3  1358 (9th Cir.1990)).  Ms. Hong’s Motion to Dismiss concerns the third element—that she 
4  falls within one of the four broad classes of PRPs.                       
5       “The four PRP classes are: ‘(1) the owner and operator of a vessel or a facility, (2) 
6  any person who at the time of disposal of any hazardous substance owned or operated any 
7  facility at which such hazardous substances were disposed of, (3) any person who by 
8  contract, agreement, or otherwise arranged for disposal or treatment, or arranged with a 
9  transporter for transport for disposal or treatment, of hazardous substances owned or 
10  possessed by such person, by any other party or entity, at any facility or incineration vessel 
11  owned or operated by another party or entity and containing such hazardous substances, 
12  and (4) any person who accepts or accepted any hazardous substances for transport to 
13  disposal or treatment facilities, incineration vessels or sites selected by such person ....’”  
14  Id. at 982 (quoting 42 U.S.C. § 9607(a)).                                 
15       The first PRP class—“the owner and operator of a vessel or a facility”—refers to 
16  current owners or operators.  California Dep’t of Toxic Substances Control v. Hearthside 
17  Residential Corp., 613 F.3d 910, 912–13 (9th Cir. 2010) (citations omitted).  In contrast, 
18  the second PRP class—“any person who at the time of disposal of any hazardous substance 
19  ... operated any facility at which such hazardous substances were disposed of”—refers to 
20  prior owners and operators of the facility.  United States v. Sterling Centrecorp Inc., 977 
21  F.3d 750, 756 (9th Cir. 2020) (citation omitted).  “To sharpen the definition [of ‘operator’] 
22  for [the] purposes of CERCLA’s concern with environmental contamination, an operator 
23  must  manage,  direct,  or  conduct  operations  specifically  related  to  pollution,  that  is, 
24  operations having to do with the leakage or disposal of hazardous waste, or decisions about 
25  compliance with environmental regulations.”  United States v. Bestfoods, 524 U.S. 51, 66–
26  67 (1998).                                                                
27       Here,  the  Hortman  Parties  allege  that  Ms.  Hong  has  owned  and  operated  the 
28  drycleaning business located at the 1654 Property since approximately December 25, 2001.  
1  (Hortman Parties’ Third-Party Complaint ¶ 14.)  The Hortman Parties also allege that Ms. 
2  Hong used PCE on the 1654 Property until 2013, before which she received notices of 
3  violation for PCE “vapor leaks” in 2003 and 2004, and a PCE “leak” in 2005.  (Id. ¶¶ 62, 
4  68.)  Ms. Hong asserts that the Hortman Parties’ use of the word “operate” in their Third-
5  Party Complaint is not sufficient to adequately allege that Ms. Hong is a member of the 
6  first PRP class—“the owner and operator of a vessel or a facility.”  In support of this 
7  argument, Ms. Hong cites only to the general proposition that the Court need not accept as 
8  true “threadbare recitals of a cause of action’s elements, supported by mere conclusory 
9  statements.”  (Doc. 223 at 15, n.4 (citing Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 663).)  The Court is not 
10  persuaded.  While the terms “operate,” “operates,” and “operator” are used and defined in 
11  the statute, they also have a factual meaning easily understood by the Court.  Therefore, 
12  the Court finds that the Hortman Parties’ allegation that Ms. Hong has owned and operated 
13  the drycleaning business located at the 1654 Property since approximately December 25, 
14  2001 is a factual allegation that is neither conclusory nor a mere recitation of CERCLA’s 
15  elements.                                                                 
16       Accordingly, the Court finds that the Hortman Parties’ allegation that Ms. Hong has 
17  owned and operated the drycleaning business since 2001, coupled with specific allegations 
18  regarding her use of PCE, are sufficient to establish that Ms. Hong was an owner or 
19  operator of the drycleaning facility at this stage.  Because Ms. Hong need only be “within 
20  one of the four broad classes of [PRPs] listed in 42 U.S.C. § 9607(a)(1)–(4),” Pakootas, 
21  830 F.3d at 981 (emphasis added), the Court need not address Ms. Hong’s remaining 
22  arguments regarding her status as a “person who at the time of disposal of any hazardous 
23  substance  owned  or  operated  any  facility  at  which  such  hazardous  substances  were 
24  disposed of,” i.e., a past owner or operator.  42 U.S.C. § 9607(a)(2).1   
25                                                                            

26

   asserted therein, which it does not (see Wright & Miller, 5C Fed. Prac. & Proc. Civ. § 1366,

1                                  IV.    CONCLUSION 
2         Based on the foregoing, Ms. Hong’s Motion to Dismiss is DENIED. 
3         IT IS SO ORDERED.

25                         II.  LEGAL STANDARD                                
26       Pursuant to Rule 12(b)(6), an action may be dismissed for failure to allege “enough 
27  facts to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.”  Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550
28 U.S. 544
, 570 (2007).  “A claim has facial plausibility when the plaintiff pleads factual 
1  content that allows the court to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is liable 
2  for  the  misconduct  alleged.   The  plausibility  standard  is  not  akin to a 
3  probability requirement, but it asks for more than a sheer possibility that a defendant acted 
4  unlawfully.”  Ashcroft v. Iqbal,
556 U.S. 662, 678
 (2009) (internal quotation marks and 
5  citations omitted).  For purposes of ruling on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, the Court “accept[s] 
6  factual allegations in the complaint as true and construe[s] the pleadings in the light most 
7  favorable to the nonmoving party.”  Manzarek v. St. Paul Fire & Marine Ins. Co.,
519 F.3d 8 1025, 1031
 (9th Cir. 2008).                                               
9       However, the Court is “not bound to accept as true a legal conclusion couched as a 
10  factual allegation.”  Iqbal,
556 U.S. at 678
 (quoting Twombly, 550 U.S. at 555).  Nor is the 
11  Court  “required  to  accept  as  true  allegations  that  contradict  exhibits  attached  to  the 
12  [c]omplaint or matters properly subject to judicial notice, or allegations that are merely 
13  conclusory, unwarranted deductions of fact, or unreasonable inferences.”  Daniels-Hall v. 
14  Nat’l Educ. Ass’n,
629 F.3d 992, 998
 (9th Cir. 2010).  “In sum, for a complaint to survive 
15  a motion to dismiss, the non-conclusory factual content, and reasonable inferences from 
16  that content, must be plausibly suggestive of a claim entitling the plaintiff to relief.”  Moss 
17  v. U.S. Secret Serv.,
572 F.3d 962, 969
 (9th Cir. 2009) (quotation marks omitted). 
18       When a Rule 12(b)(6) motion is granted, “a district court should grant leave to amend 
19  even if no request to amend the pleading was made, unless it determines that the pleading 
20  could not possibly be cured by the allegation of other facts.”  Cook, Perkiss & Liehe v. N. 
21  Cal. Collection Serv.,
911 F.2d 242
, 247 (9th Cir. 1990) (citations omitted).   
22                            III.  DISCUSSION                                
23       “In order to prevail in a private action under CERCLA for response costs or natural 
24  resource damages, a plaintiff must prove the following elements, among others: (1) the site 
25  on  which  the  hazardous  substances  are  found  is  a  ‘facility’  within  the  meaning  of 
26  CERCLA,
42 U.S.C. § 9601
(9); (2) a ‘release’ or ‘threatened release’ of any ‘hazardous 
27  substance’ from the facility has occurred,
42 U.S.C. § 9607
(a)(4); and (3) the defendant is 
28  within one of the four broad classes of ‘potentially responsible parties’ (‘PRPs’) listed in 
1
42 U.S.C. § 9607
(a)(1)–(4).”  Pakootas v. Teck Cominco Metals, LTD.,
830 F.3d 975
, 981 
2  (9th Cir. 2016) (citing 3550 Stevens Creek Assocs. v. Barclays Bank of Cal.,
915 F.2d 1355
, 
3  1358 (9th Cir.1990)).  Ms. Hong’s Motion to Dismiss concerns the third element—that she 
4  falls within one of the four broad classes of PRPs.                       
5       “The four PRP classes are: ‘(1) the owner and operator of a vessel or a facility, (2) 
6  any person who at the time of disposal of any hazardous substance owned or operated any 
7  facility at which such hazardous substances were disposed of, (3) any person who by 
8  contract, agreement, or otherwise arranged for disposal or treatment, or arranged with a 
9  transporter for transport for disposal or treatment, of hazardous substances owned or 
10  possessed by such person, by any other party or entity, at any facility or incineration vessel 
11  owned or operated by another party or entity and containing such hazardous substances, 
12  and (4) any person who accepts or accepted any hazardous substances for transport to 
13  disposal or treatment facilities, incineration vessels or sites selected by such person ....’”  
14
Id.
 at 982 (quoting
42 U.S.C. § 9607
(a)).                                 
15       The first PRP class—“the owner and operator of a vessel or a facility”—refers to 
16  current owners or operators.  California Dep’t of Toxic Substances Control v. Hearthside 
17  Residential Corp.,
613 F.3d 910
, 912–13 (9th Cir. 2010) (citations omitted).  In contrast, 
18  the second PRP class—“any person who at the time of disposal of any hazardous substance 
19  ... operated any facility at which such hazardous substances were disposed of”—refers to 
20  prior owners and operators of the facility.  United States v. Sterling Centrecorp Inc., 977
21 F.3d 750, 756
 (9th Cir. 2020) (citation omitted).  “To sharpen the definition [of ‘operator’] 
22  for [the] purposes of CERCLA’s concern with environmental contamination, an operator 
23  must  manage,  direct,  or  conduct  operations  specifically  related  to  pollution,  that  is, 
24  operations having to do with the leakage or disposal of hazardous waste, or decisions about 
25  compliance with environmental regulations.”  United States v. Bestfoods,
524 U.S. 51
, 66–
26  67 (1998).                                                                
27       Here,  the  Hortman  Parties  allege  that  Ms.  Hong  has  owned  and  operated  the 
28  drycleaning business located at the 1654 Property since approximately December 25, 2001.  
1  (Hortman Parties’ Third-Party Complaint ¶ 14.)  The Hortman Parties also allege that Ms. 
2  Hong used PCE on the 1654 Property until 2013, before which she received notices of 
3  violation for PCE “vapor leaks” in 2003 and 2004, and a PCE “leak” in 2005.  (Id. ¶¶ 62, 
4  68.)  Ms. Hong asserts that the Hortman Parties’ use of the word “operate” in their Third-
5  Party Complaint is not sufficient to adequately allege that Ms. Hong is a member of the 
6  first PRP class—“the owner and operator of a vessel or a facility.”  In support of this 
7  argument, Ms. Hong cites only to the general proposition that the Court need not accept as 
8  true “threadbare recitals of a cause of action’s elements, supported by mere conclusory 
9  statements.”  (Doc. 223 at 15, n.4 (citing Iqbal,
556 U.S. at 663
).)  The Court is not 
10  persuaded.  While the terms “operate,” “operates,” and “operator” are used and defined in 
11  the statute, they also have a factual meaning easily understood by the Court.  Therefore, 
12  the Court finds that the Hortman Parties’ allegation that Ms. Hong has owned and operated 
13  the drycleaning business located at the 1654 Property since approximately December 25, 
14  2001 is a factual allegation that is neither conclusory nor a mere recitation of CERCLA’s 
15  elements.                                                                 
16       Accordingly, the Court finds that the Hortman Parties’ allegation that Ms. Hong has 
17  owned and operated the drycleaning business since 2001, coupled with specific allegations 
18  regarding her use of PCE, are sufficient to establish that Ms. Hong was an owner or 
19  operator of the drycleaning facility at this stage.  Because Ms. Hong need only be “within 
20  one of the four broad classes of [PRPs] listed in
42 U.S.C. § 9607
(a)(1)–(4),” Pakootas, 
21
830 F.3d at 981
 (emphasis added), the Court need not address Ms. Hong’s remaining 
22  arguments regarding her status as a “person who at the time of disposal of any hazardous 
23  substance  owned  or  operated  any  facility  at  which  such  hazardous  substances  were 
24  disposed of,” i.e., a past owner or operator.
42 U.S.C. § 9607
(a)(2).1
